title: Count evaluated expressions in C
description:
Stacked on #733.

Instrumented code now calls `.Call(covr:::covr_count, <index>L, "<key>")` instead of `covr:::count(key)`. The `.Call` primitive itself is embedded in the call, so a `.Call` defined where the traced function lives can't mask it. Primitives serialize by name, and the embedded primitive costs ~9 ns more than plain `.Call`. `src/count.c` keeps a growable array of counts and a parallel array of the trace keys.

- **Fast path:** when the index belongs to the key (a pointer comparison of the interned key), the count is incremented in C.
- **Fallback:** otherwise, e.g. in a worker that unserialized an instrumented function, it calls `covr:::count(key)`, as before.
- **Syncing:** `sync_counts()` adds the pending C counts to `.counters[[key]]$value`. It's called wherever counts are read: `save_trace()`, `as_coverage()`, `collect_coverage()` and the Shiny path. `clear_counters()` and `zero_counters()` reset the C counts.
- **Fallback namespace:** covr's namespace is looked up on each fallback, so counts still land in the right place after covr is unloaded and loaded again.
- **Recording tests:** with `covr.record_tests = TRUE`, code still calls `count_and_record()` (the R path).

## Numbers (R 4.6.2)

| | #733 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Overhead per count (microbenchmark) | ~530 ns | ~95 ns |
| Luminescence 0.9.25 instrumented tests, median of 3 interleaved runs | 139.1 s | 126.3 s (−9%) |
| `sync_counts()` with 16,158 counters pending | | 0.49 s |

Counts are identical: Luminescence gives 19,849,462 with both. forcats and checkmate coverage is identical through `package_coverage()`, apart from traces in checkmate's randomized tests. A traced function sent to a callr worker runs correctly through the fallback.

This mainly pays off with branch coverage (#279), which adds one count per evaluated `if`, about 1.4x as many calls.


Rebased onto the branch coverage from main (#730). Branch counters stay in R; `without_index()` skips `.counters$branches`. Moving branch counting to C as well is a possible follow-up.

title: Fix coverage bugs and simplify covr internals
description:
## Overview

Combines the self-coverage review and simplicity audit. Includes the Coveralls CI autodetection work previously proposed in #731, which is folded into this PR.

## Fixes

- Give imputed source references consistent counter keys across processes with different `keep.parse.data` settings, avoiding false uncovered conditions.
- Count braceless `while` bodies separately from their conditions.
- Skip active bindings when finding functions, R6 classes, S7 objects, box modules and S4 methods to instrument.
- Make failed `system_output()` commands catchable by ordinary error handlers.
- Evaluate `package_coverage(combine_types = FALSE)` arguments in the caller’s frame.
- Check that rstudioapi is installed before using its source-marker API.
- Detect the CI service in `coveralls()`, handle a NULL repository token, and use GitHub Actions environment metadata without requiring an origin remote.

## Simplification and compatibility changes

- Remove Intel classic icc support and its options.
- Remove Wercker, Codeship and Semaphore Classic detection, and the deprecated `exclusions` argument.
- Deprecate `pre_clean` and `azure()`.
- Replace the internal markers S3 generic with a plain source-marker helper.
- Remove unused helpers, arguments, duplicate definitions and unreachable branches.
- Share tracing, trace merging, unsaved-trace warnings, percentage/threshold handling and exporter code.

## Verification

- Added regression and behavioral tests across coverage entry points, compiled-code processing, exporters, reports, test recording and object traversal.
- Installed the combined version into a temporary library and ran the full suite with `NOT_CRAN=true`: passed.
- Self-coverage after rebasing the first three commits onto main was 95.88%. This measurement predates the four simplicity-audit commits; the final combined branch has not been remeasured.
- Documented the intentional loss of self-coverage in the SIGKILL regression test.

title: Add opt-in branch coverage of R code (#279)
description:
Adds experimental, opt-in branch coverage of R code (#279), following the design notes in `branch-coverage-design.md` (b07fa14) and the maintainer decisions on scope.

## Usage

```r
options(covr.branch_coverage = TRUE)
cov <- package_coverage()
tally_coverage(cov, by = "branch")   # one row per branch
percent_coverage(cov, by = "branch")
to_lcov(cov)                          # BRDA / BRF / BRH
to_cobertura(cov)                     # branch-rate, condition-coverage
```

Documented in `?covr.branch_coverage` (marked experimental), the options list in `?covr`, `?coverage`, `?tally_coverage`, `?to_lcov` and `?to_cobertura`.

## What counts as a branch

- `if`: `"TRUE"` and `"FALSE"`, including the implicit `else` of an `if` without one. `else if` chains are separate decisions.
- `switch()`: one branch per arm, labelled by name. Arms that fall through (`a = , b = 2`) share one branch (`"a, b"`). An unnamed arm is `"<default>"`, or its position when all arms are unnamed (numeric switches). A `switch()` without a default gets an added `covr:::branch_miss(key)` default that counts `"<no match>"` and returns `invisible(NULL)`, like an unmatched `switch()`. A default is not added when it would change behavior: a single unnamed arm is the default of a character `EXPR`, so only all-named switches, or all-unnamed switches with 2+ arms, get one. Switches with `...` arms or a trailing empty arm are left alone. The added default only catches a numeric `EXPR` of `n + 1`, so with an added default `EXPR` is wrapped as `covr:::branch_switch(key, EXPR, n)`. For a non-character `EXPR` that selects no arm (0, negative, past the end, `NA`), it counts `"<no match>"`; whether an arm is selected is decided by `switch()` itself, using an inlined probe. It returns `EXPR` unchanged.
- Not included yet: `&&`/`||`, loops, compiled code.

## Instrumentation (approach A)

`if (cond)` becomes `if (covr:::branch(key, cond))`. `branch()` records the branch and returns `cond` unchanged, so `if` itself raises its errors and warnings. Classed objects always go through the slow path, so `length()`/`is.na()` methods are never dispatched (`if` doesn't dispatch them). For conditions other than a scalar `TRUE`/`FALSE`, the branch is found by evaluating `if (cond)` inside `tryCatch()`, so numbers, `"T"`/`"false"` and factors are counted the way `if` reads them. `NA`, length 0, length > 1 and non-logical conditions record nothing. Nothing is recorded if `cond` itself errors. Tests compare the condition class and message with uninstrumented R. Switch arms are wrapped as `if (TRUE) { covr:::branch_arm(key, i); <arm> }`, which keeps visibility.

**No cost when off.** `trace_calls()` reads the option at instrumentation time, only for conditionals that have srcrefs. When the option is off, instrumentation is exactly what it was. `test-branches.R` instruments a fixture of `if`/`switch`/loop/nested/braceless constructs and checks the traced bodies are `identical()` to `tests/testthat/branches/instrumentation-main.rds`. That file was generated with `origin/main` (3b9ccf0), with the option unset and with it `FALSE`. The rest of the `trace_calls()` change is a small restructure that computes the decision's srcref once. It makes the same `impute_srcref()` calls as before.

For `package_coverage()` the option is passed to the R subprocesses by an onLoad hook, like `covr.record_tests` and `covr.full_traversal`. I didn't add a `package_coverage()` argument: none of the other instrumentation options have one, so an option fits better.

## Data model

Branches go in a separate store, so line and expression coverage don't change:

- At run time: `.counters$branches`, an environment keyed like counters (`key(srcref)` of the `if`/`switch()`). Each entry has `srcref`, `functions`, `labels` and `value` (one count per branch).
- In a coverage object: `attr(cov, "branches")`, a sorted named list of those entries. Objects made without the option are unchanged: there is no attribute.

The store is carried through:

- trace files written by finalizers (`save_trace()`/`portable_srcfiles()` serialize it with `.counters`)
- `merge_coverage()` (summed by key)
- `c()` for coverage objects
- forked workers: `trace_forks()` zeroes branch counts after a fork, and `fix_mcexit()` saves them
- `covr.record_tests` (branches are counted alongside test recording, but not recorded per test)
- `exclude()`: `# nocov` on the decision's first line, file and line exclusions, `.covrignore` and `function_exclusions` drop all its branches
- `[.coverage`: subsetting a coverage object keeps the decisions that contain a retained trace (e.g. the trace of the condition), so `cov[0]` has no branches. This also covers `filter_non_package_files()`.
- relative paths

The reserved `branches` element is read with `[[` rather than `$`, because `$` would partially match a trace key in a file named `branches*.R`. That happens for covr's own `R/branches.R` under self-coverage.

`tally_tests()` (#723, now on main) works on coverage with branches; branch hits aren't recorded per test, so it reports lines only.


## Conditionals in argument defaults

#682 imputes srcrefs for braceless conditionals in function bodies and calls, but not in argument defaults. Formals were traced with no srcref at all, so `function(x = if (y) 1 else 2)` had neither line counters nor branches for its arms. `trace_formals()` now traces each default with an `impute_ref` built from the function's parse data: `impute_formal_srcrefs()` takes the `expr` after each `SYMBOL_FORMALS EQ_FORMALS`. As in #682, the parse data is only looked up, once per function, when a conditional in a default needs it. Defaults without conditionals are traced exactly as before, and a test checks this. This changes reported line coverage whether or not branch coverage is on, the way #682 did: a default whose branch never ran no longer counts as covered. It has its own NEWS bullet. Defaults of `function` definitions nested inside a body still aren't imputed, again as in #682.

## Outputs

- **`to_lcov()`**: `BRDA:<line>,<block>,<branch>,<taken>` on the line where the decision starts, then `BRF`/`BRH`. These come after `FN*` and before `DA`, as in geninfo(1). `block` numbers the decisions on a line from 0, which geninfo requires. `branch` is a 0-based integer. `taken` is `-` when the decision never ran (all its counts are 0), as the spec defines `-`, and otherwise the count. Nothing changes without the option.
- **`to_cobertura()`**: real `branch-rate`, `branches-covered` and `branches-valid`. Lines with decisions get `branch="true" condition-coverage="50% (1/2)"`, as in coverage-04.dtd (`branch`, `condition-coverage`). As in coverage.py, the branch rate of code without branches is `1`. Without the option the output is byte-identical; the existing `cobertura.xml` comparison test still passes.
- **`percent_coverage(by = "branch")`** / **`tally_coverage(by = "branch")`**: the data frame has columns `filename`, `functions`, `line`, `column`, `branch`, `label` and `value`.
- **`codecov()`**: Codecov's R format (`"uploader": "R"`, read by `RlangProcessor`) calls `int(cov)` on every value ([rlang.py](https://github.com/codecov/umbrella/blob/005cc3a12f34cd1d4d78a08cef13b90a012c313e/apps/worker/services/report/languages/rlang.py)), so it can't carry branches. With branch coverage, the report body therefore uses Codecov's [generic JSON format](https://docs.codecov.com/docs/codecov-custom-coverage-format), `{"coverage": {"R/f.R": [null, 1, "1/2", ...]}}`, with no `uploader` key, which would otherwise route it to the R processor. Lines with decisions get `"taken/total"` summed over the decisions on the line; [v1.py](https://github.com/codecov/umbrella/blob/005cc3a12f34cd1d4d78a08cef13b90a012c313e/apps/worker/services/report/languages/v1.py) turns those strings into branch lines. The endpoint and upload envelope don't change, and without the option the report is still the R format, byte for byte. Codecov counts a partly covered line as not covered in its percentage, which is documented. Longer term we could ask Codecov to extend the R format to take branches.
- **`coveralls()`**: each source file gets `branches: [line, block, branch, hits, ...]` from the [/jobs API](https://docs.coveralls.io/api-jobs-endpoint), numbered as in `to_lcov()`. Never-taken branches send `0`, as Coveralls' own reporters do. Files without branches, and every file when the option is off, have no `branches` key. The `coveralls()` docs now say to upload `to_lcov()` output when using the Coveralls GitHub Action with branch coverage.
- **Not yet**: `to_sonarqube()`, `report()`, `file_report()`.

LCOV and Coveralls share `branch_blocks()`, which numbers the decisions on each line.

I haven't tried a live upload to Codecov or Coveralls; the formats are checked against their source and docs.

## Performance

`package_coverage()` wall time in seconds, median of 5 interleaved runs. Install and test run are included. Pure-R CRAN packages, R 4.4.3, WSL2:

| Package (R lines, `if`s) | main | branch, option off | branch, option on |
|---|---|---|---|
| pillar 1.11.1 (6.7k, 356) | 14.13 | 14.27 | 15.16 (+7%) |
| scales 1.4.0 (7.4k, 342) | 9.28 | 9.11 | 9.59 (+3%) |

These numbers are from the quieter of two runs, taken before the `branch()` fast path was inlined. A second run with the final code was noisier (other jobs on the machine, ±15% between repeats): pillar 15.73 / 14.36 / 14.79, scales 9.21 / 10.17 / 9.61. Most of the wall time is installing the package. Line coverage (pillar 83.14%, scales 82.04%) is the same in every configuration. Branch coverage is 74.00% (677 branches) for pillar and 73.75% (518) for scales.

With the option off, timings are within noise of main, as expected since the instrumented code is identical. With it on, the overhead was 3–7% of the total `package_coverage()` time for these packages.

Per-call cost, from 1e6 calls in a loop: `branch()` with a scalar logical takes about 1.3 µs on top of a no-op closure call (about 0.2 µs). An `if` instrumented for lines only already costs about 0.6 µs per counter. I inlined the fast path (no `isTRUE()` or helper calls) after the first benchmark showed about 2 µs.

## Tests

New `test-branches.R` covers:

- instrumentation identical with the option off
- `if` and implicit `else` counts
- `switch` fall-through, default, numeric and `"<no match>"` arms
- visibility and value of `switch()`
- `...` switches
- identical conditions signalled by `if` for `NA`, `logical()`, `c(TRUE, FALSE)`, `"yes"` and `list(TRUE)`, with nothing recorded, including when the condition errors
- conditions `if` coerces
- `missing()`/`nargs()`/`sys.call()` in conditions
- line coverage unchanged by the option
- `percent_coverage(by = "branch")`
- trace file save and merge, with `zero_counters()`
- `c()`
- forked processes
- `covr.record_tests`
- end-to-end `package_coverage()` on a new `TestBranches` fixture (with `# nocov` and a forked process)

There are also new LCOV, Cobertura, Codecov, Coveralls and exclusion tests. The Codecov and Coveralls tests check both the branch payloads and that the payloads without branch coverage are unchanged.

- Full suite with this branch installed first (`R CMD INSTALL -l $lib .`, `R_LIBS=$lib`): `[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 993 ]`.
- Self-coverage with `shim_package.sh` on a `git archive` copy: tests pass, 71.93% (measured after rebasing onto main with #723–#726, which added code that self-coverage reaches less of; before the rebase it was 76.69%, against 75.33% on main). Main shows the same "Can't find coverage from 2 R processes that loaded covrShim" warning, so it isn't new.

This targets covr 4.0.0.

title: Measure the coverage of Rust code
description:
Fixes #728.

`package_coverage()` now measures the coverage of the Rust code in a package's `src/`, such as the code of packages using extendr or savvy. Before this change only the C glue code (e.g. `src/entrypoint.c`) was reported.

## How it works

Rust code is built by cargo into a static library, which is linked into the package's shared object. gcov can't read it, so covr uses LLVM's source-based coverage (`-C instrument-coverage`):

1. **Instrument.** When `src/` has a `Cargo.toml` (outside `vendor/`, `target/` and `.cargo/`), covr sets `RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER` to a small script that cargo runs instead of rustc for the crates of the package's workspace. The script adds `-C instrument-coverage`. This works however the package sets `RUSTFLAGS`:
   - extendr's `RUSTFLAGS="$(RUSTFLAGS) …"`
   - savvy's `RUSTFLAGS =`
   - clarabel's `export RUSTFLAGS="-C linker=…"`
   - automerge, which runs cargo in `configure`

   It doesn't override rustflags in cargo's config either. Dependencies aren't instrumented, so they build exactly as without covr, and their build cache is reused. The script only instruments code compiled by the toolchain covr checked. It logs what it compiled, so covr can warn when the code was built by another toolchain or wasn't compiled by cargo at all (e.g. a prebuilt library).
2. **Link the profiler runtime.** A Rust **staticlib doesn't bundle `profiler_builtins`**, and on Linux LLVM doesn't emit a reference to it. Without this step the `.so` has counters but nothing writes them, and every line reports 0. covr adds the toolchain's `libprofiler_builtins-*.rlib` to `PKG_LIBS`, plus `-Wl,-u,__llvm_profile_runtime` on Linux.
3. **Collect.** `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<install_path>/rust_profiles/%p-%m.profraw` is set for the processes that run vignettes, examples, tests and `code`. Profiles written during install (instrumented proc macros, build scripts, the load test) go to a throwaway directory.
4. **Read.** `llvm-profdata merge -sparse` → `llvm-cov export -format=lcov` on the installed shared object → `SF:`/`DA:` records parsed into line coverages. Only files in the package (or `covr.gcov_additional_paths`) are kept.
5. **Leave out dependencies.** For packages with Rust code, files in `vendor/`, `target/` and `.cargo/` directories are dropped. This covers both Rust files and the C code that vendored crates compile, which gcov would otherwise measure. For example, string2path compiles savvy's `unwind_protect_wrapper.c` with the cc crate.

### Finding the llvm tools

`llvm-cov` and `llvm-profdata` must match rustc's LLVM major version. covr checks, in order:

- **rustup:** the toolchain's `rustup component add llvm-tools`, under `$(rustc --print sysroot)/lib/rustlib/<host>/bin`.
- **Rust from a Linux distribution** (`apt-get install cargo rustc`, as CRAN's [Using Rust in CRAN packages](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/using_rust.html) recommends): these builds use the system LLVM and ship the profiler runtime, but not llvm-tools. covr looks on the `PATH` for `llvm-cov-<N>` (Debian/Ubuntu naming), or for an `llvm-cov` whose `--version` reports the same major version as `rustc -vV` (e.g. Fedora).
- **Where rustc is found:** the `PATH` first, then `$CARGO_HOME/bin` or `~/.cargo/bin`, as the CRAN document asks `configure` scripts to do. rustc is resolved in `src/`, where packages run cargo, so the same `rust-toolchain.toml` applies. For example, eulerr pins 1.88 in `src/rust/`, which cargo run from `src/` ignores. If covr had resolved rustc in `src/rust/` instead, it would link 1.88's profiler runtime into code built by the default toolchain, which segfaults when the package loads.

## Behavior and options

- If the llvm tools or the profiler runtime are missing, covr **warns and skips the Rust code** without instrumenting it. Existing Rust packages keep working without the tools. The warning names what's missing and the LLVM version to install.
- `options(covr.llvm_cov = "")` turns Rust coverage off. `covr.llvm_cov` and `covr.llvm_profdata` set the tool paths.
- If `llvm-profdata` or `llvm-cov` fails, covr warns with the tool's output and returns the rest of the coverage. This happens, for example, when a Makevars drops `RUSTFLAGS` (llvm-cov then reports `no coverage data found`), or when a package links a prebuilt library instead of building from source.

## Checks

### Popular CRAN packages with Rust code

These are the most-downloaded of the 94 CRAN packages that list cargo/rustc, plus every one maintained at Posit. I ran each with `package_coverage(allow_failures = TRUE)` and `NOT_CRAN=true`, on Linux with rustc 1.99:

| Package | Maintainer | Binding | Time | Rust lines covered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gifski | Jeroen Ooms | C FFI | 14 s | 0 / 0, no warning. Its own crate only re-exports the gifski crate |
| clarabel | B. Narasimhan | savvy, `export RUSTFLAGS=` in the recipe | 23 s | 334 / 440 |
| eulerr | Johan Larsson | extendr, pinned `rust-toolchain.toml` | 59 s | 1295 / 1452 |
| fru | M. Kursa | C FFI | 9 s | 929 / 1275. Needs R ≥ 4.5 (`Rf_asBool`), so run on R 4.6.2 |
| yaml12 | T. Kalinowski (Posit) | savvy | 62 s | 1397 / 1549. Run twice in a row, same result |
| tinyimg | Yihui Xie | extendr | 22 s | 266 / 305 |
| arcgisutils | Josiah Parry | extendr | 18 s | 22 / 1897. Most tests need ArcGIS credentials; one needs udunits, which isn't installed here |
| waysign | T. L. Pedersen (Posit) | extendr | 9 s | 21 / 57 |
| ggsql | T. L. Pedersen (Posit) | extendr, with DuckDB/Arrow/ODBC | 998 s | 234 / 286. Long because the dependency tree is huge; built with `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2` to fit in 6 GB |
| tok | T. Kalinowski (Posit) | extendr | 54 s | 471 / 641 |
| automerge | C. Gao (Posit) | C bindings; Rust built in `configure` | 55 s | 15308 / 28598. This is the bundled upstream automerge library, which counts like bundled C code; `.covrignore` can drop it |

clarabel and automerge got no Rust coverage with the earlier `RUSTFLAGS` make-variable approach, and eulerr segfaulted on load. The current wrapper approach fixed all three. I found no other Posit R packages with Rust in their `src/` (searched posit-dev, r-lib, tidyverse and rstudio). posit-dev/hephaestus-r is a small exception, isn't on CRAN, and wasn't tested.

**r-polars** (pola-rs/r-polars main, v2.1.0.9000, built from source with `LIBR_POLARS_BUILD=true`) was the stress test:

- **First run:** 17.7 min total, of which 16 min is cargo. All 4328 tests pass, there are no warnings, and 5610 / 6360 lines in 55 Rust files are covered.
- **Second run:** 3.2 min. cargo only recompiles the `r-polars` crate (1 min 48 s), because the wrapper leaves polars and the other dependencies cached.
- **R coverage:** 61% by default, 88% with `options(covr.full_traversal = TRUE)`. polars defines its expression methods inside environments, and covr doesn't trace those by default. The package can enable it with `Config/covr/full_traversal: true`. This is unrelated to the Rust support.

### Other checks

All local runs were on Linux.

- **CRAN packages:**

  | Package | Binding / layout | Rust coverage reported |
  |---|---|---|
  | b64 0.1.7 | extendr template, `lto = true`, vendor in `src/vendor` (removed after build) | `lib.rs` 18.46% (tests) |
  | hellorust 1.2.3 | plain C FFI + `wrapper.c` | `hello.rs`, `random.rs`, `mythreads.rs` 100% (examples) |
  | prqlr 0.10.1 | savvy, `cargo build --target=…` | `lib.rs` 40.91% (tests) |
  | string2path 0.3.1 (the example in CRAN's Rust document; now archived) | savvy, vendored crates kept in `src/rust/vendor`, `target/` kept, `CARGO_HOME=src/.cargo` | `lib.rs` 53%, `builder.rs` 60.8%, `font.rs` 30%, `into_path.rs` 90.6%, `result.rs` 91.1%, `into_fill_stroke.rs` 96.9%. No vendored crates, and no savvy C files after the dependency filter |

  Notes on two of these runs:
  - **string2path:** needs fontconfig's pkg-config file, which isn't installed on this machine, so I supplied a stub `.pc`.
  - **prqlr:** `test-knitr-engine.R:26` fails under covr (`object 'con' not found`) with or without Rust instrumentation, so I ran it with `allow_failures = TRUE`.
- **extendr and savvy, current templates:**

  | Package | Rust files reported | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | Fresh `rextendr::use_extendr()` scaffold (rextendr 0.5.0) with a `sign()` function and test | `lib.rs` 88.9%, exact branch counts | Also run twice with `DEBUG=true`, where the `target/` dir is kept |
  | extendr's own `tests/extendrtests` (current `main`) | 24 files: `lib.rs`, `altrep.rs`, `externalptr.rs`, `dataframe.rs`, … | |
  | savvy's own `R-package` (savvyExamples, current `main`, the `savvy-cli init` template) | 22 files: `altrep.rs`, `numeric.rs`, `error_handling.rs`, … | Run twice in a row, giving the same results (8.7 s, then 3.5 s with cargo's cache) |

  This testing found two bugs, now fixed and covered by tests:
  1. **savvy's template dropped the instrumentation.** Its Makevars sets `RUSTFLAGS =` and overrides the environment variable, so the first version of this PR reported `no coverage data found`. The rustc wrapper (see above) replaced the environment variable. The `TestRust` fixture's Makevars sets `RUSTFLAGS` itself, like savvy and clarabel, and its tests fail with the old approach.
  2. **A second `package_coverage()` failed for packages that keep cargo's `target/`.** `clean_objects()` deleted every `.a` under `src/`, including the archives that build scripts put in `target/` (savvy's `libunwind_protect.a`). cargo doesn't notice that they're gone, so the next build fails with `could not find native static library unwind_protect`. This also happens with covr on `main`. For packages with Rust code, `clean_objects()` now leaves `target/`, `vendor/` and `.cargo/` alone.

  Code generated by `#[extendr]` and `#[savvy]` is attributed to the macro's line, as in `llvm-cov show`. For example, extendr's wrapper closure that handles failed argument conversion is reported on the `#[extendr]` line. So those lines show as not covered unless such paths run. Users can exclude them with `// # nocov`. This is documented in `?package_coverage`, and covr doesn't filter these lines.
- **Distribution toolchain:** I extracted Ubuntu 24.04's `rustc`, `cargo`, `libstd-rust-dev` (1.75.0, LLVM 17) and `llvm-17` packages without installing them. covr found `/usr/bin/llvm-cov-17` and Ubuntu's `libprofiler_builtins`, and the `TestRust` line counts match the rustup toolchain (1.99, LLVM 23) exactly. Debian's `debian/rules` builds rustc with `profiler = true` on most architectures, and Fedora's spec links `libclang_rt.profile`.
- **Tests:** `test-rust.R` uses a new dependency-free `TestRust` fixture (staticlib + C wrapper). It checks:
  - exact line counts in `lib.rs`
  - the `covr.llvm_cov = ""` opt-out
  - the warnings for missing tools and a missing runtime
  - an llvm-cov failure
  - matching system llvm tools by version (fake tool scripts on `PATH`)
  - LCOV parsing
  - dropping vendored Rust and C files, including when the package itself is in a directory named `vendor`

  The full suite passes locally: 944 tests, 0 skipped.
- **CI:** both workflows now run `rustup component add llvm-tools` (except on Windows), so the Rust tests run in CI rather than being skipped. The Rust tests ran and passed on ubuntu and **macOS** (`macos-latest`, no skips besides the existing gcov JSON ones).

## Limitations

- **Not available on Windows.** covr warns and skips the Rust code there. On the first CI run, covr skipped the Rust tests on Windows. rustup's standard library for `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`, the target Rtools builds for, ships **no `profiler_builtins`**. I checked the 1.99.0 dist tarballs: the `*-windows-gnullvm` and macOS targets include it. Rather than ship untested support for the `gnullvm` targets, which do include it, covr doesn't try on Windows. On macOS, LLVM emits the reference to the runtime itself, so only the rlib is linked.
- Packages that download a prebuilt static library, which CRAN allows when the download is checksummed, can't be instrumented. covr warns, as described above.
- Counts from processes that don't exit normally are lost, as with gcov. For example, forked `mcparallel()` workers exit with `_exit()`.
- `covr.gcov_partial` doesn't apply to Rust, because LCOV has no partial-line information.

title: Detect the CI service in coveralls()
description:
`coveralls()` defaulted to `service_name = "travis-ci"` and `service_job_id = TRAVIS_JOB_ID`, so on GitHub Actions (and every other service) it reported the upload as a Travis job unless `service_name` was passed. #687 only added git info when `service_name = "github-actions"` was set explicitly.

Now `coveralls()` reuses the CI detection of `codecov()`:

- **`service_name`** defaults to `NULL`: `CI_NAME` if it is set, otherwise the detected service, named the way Coveralls' own [coverage-reporter](https://github.com/coverallsapp/coverage-reporter/tree/master/src/coverage_reporter/ci) names it (`github`, `travis-ci`, `gitlab-ci`, `circleci`, `jenkins`, `drone`, ...), otherwise `"local"`. An explicit `service_name` (e.g. `"github-actions"`, `"travis-pro"`) is still used as is.
- **`service_job_id`** and **`service_pull_request`** come from the detected service.
- **git info**: with a `repo_token`, the commit, branch and remote are now submitted on every service. Each comes from `CI_BRANCH`/`CI_REMOTE` if set, then the CI service (on GitHub Actions the remote is built from `GITHUB_SERVER_URL`/`GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, so no `origin` remote is needed), then the local repository. Failing git commands are skipped rather than erroring, e.g. with no `origin` remote or outside a repository; if the PR head commit isn't in a shallow clone, only its id is sent.
- `repo_token = NULL` now works like `""`.
- The committer fields are now `committer_name`/`committer_email`, as in the [Coveralls API](https://docs.coveralls.io/api-jobs-endpoint); they were misspelled `commiter_*`.

Without a token, only Travis CI is accepted by Coveralls, and that payload is unchanged (`travis-ci` with `TRAVIS_JOB_ID`).

This includes the `repo_token = NULL` and GitHub Actions remote fixes that were also on the `coverage-on-coverage` branch; that branch will drop its `R/coveralls.R` changes when it is rebased.

Tested with the full test suite (with this covr installed into a temporary library), and with a smoke run of `to_coveralls()` without mocks: locally in this repo, under simulated GitHub Actions pull request variables with a commit that isn't in the clone, outside a git repository, and without a token.

title: Require R 4.0.0
description:
Supersedes #584 (the workflow updates there have since landed separately).

R 4.0.0 is ~6 years old, and covr's hard dependencies on CRAN already need R >= 3.6 (httr, withr, R6), so the declared `R (>= 3.1.0)` was not attainable from a fresh install and was never tested.

- `Depends: R (>= 4.0.0)`.
- Remove the `isNamespaceLoaded()` fallback for R < 3.2 (`R/utils.R`) and the R < 3.3 branch in `covr_reassign_function()` (`src/reassign.c`) plus the vignette sentence describing it.
- Remove a test in `test-utils.R` that only ran on R < 4.0.
- CI: replace the Windows R 3.6 (RTools35) job with Windows R 4.0 to check the minimum version.
- Update the compatibility note in `AGENTS.md` (base pipe and `\(x)` still need R 4.1, so they stay off limits).

Local: full `devtools::test()` passes on R 4.4.3 with this covr installed (803 passed, 0 failed).

title: Measure compiled code coverage in the current session
description:
Fixes #605.

`file_coverage()` can now measure a package's compiled code, as asked in the issue:

```r
file_coverage("src/foo.c", "tests/testthat/test-foo.R")
```

It loads the package with `pkgload::load_all()` and measures the coverage with gcov in the current session, so devtools isn't needed. `environment_coverage()` and `with_coverage()` also include the compiled code of packages loaded with `pkgload::load_all()`. This means `devtools::test_coverage_active_file("src/foo.c")` works with no changes to devtools: devtools already maps `src/foo.c` to `test-foo.R` and filters the coverage by file name.

## How it works

1. covr builds an instrumented copy of the package in the session's temporary directory, using `pkgbuild::compile_dll()` with `covr.flags`. The package's own `src/` is never touched. Each run copies only the files that changed (respecting `.Rbuildignore`), so only those are recompiled. A change to a header rebuilds everything, since make doesn't track headers.
2. While the code runs, the namespace's DLLs are swapped for the instrumented ones. This covers the native routine objects bound in the namespace, the `DLLs` namespace info, and string lookups by DLL name. DLLs named differently from their package, like data.table's `data_table`, are supported.
3. Unloading the instrumented DLL makes libgcov write its `.gcda` counts. `run_gcov()` reads them, the paths are mapped back to the package, and the original DLL is restored, also when the code errors.

`options(covr.gcov = "")` turns this off.

## Checks

- **Linux (gcc 13) and Windows (R 4.4.3, Rtools 44):** counts match `package_coverage()` on the `TestCompiled` fixture, including headers included by several objects.
- **data.table:** for `src/fmelt.c` with a small melt script, the counts match `package_coverage(type = "none", code = ...)` on all 586 lines both report. A warm `file_coverage()` run takes about 3 s, against about 13.5 s for `package_coverage()`.
- **devtools:** `devtools::test_coverage_active_file("src/simple.cc")` (devtools 2.5.2, unmodified) returns the C coverage. Its second run takes 0.24 s.
- **Tests:** the new tests in `test-compiled_session.R` cover `environment_coverage()`, `with_coverage()` (including restoring the DLL on error), `file_coverage()`, header changes, repeated runs not adding up counts, and `covr.gcov = ""`. The full suite passes.

## Limitations

- Native routines looked up some other way keep using the package's own DLL, so their code isn't counted. Examples: routines stored by `.onLoad()`, or found by other packages with `R_GetCCallable()`. This is documented.
- Not tested on macOS (llvm-cov). The flush on `dyn.unload()` there is unverified.

title: Add `tally_tests()` traceability matrix
description:
`tally_tests()` turns coverage recorded with `options(covr.record_tests = TRUE)` into a data frame with one row for each line of code and each test that ran it: the test file and line (relative to the package for `package_coverage()`), the `test_that()`/`it()` description, and the number of times the test ran the line. Lines match `tally_coverage(by = "line")`.

Fixes #361.

title: Add shiny_app_coverage() for Shiny apps outside of packages
description:
Follow-up to #719, which added `vignette("shiny")`. Fixes #277.

New `shiny_app_coverage()` measures the coverage of a Shiny app that isn't part of a package, including the code run by the app in the R processes that shinytest2 starts:

```r
shiny_app_coverage(app_dir = ".", code = shinytest2::test_app(app_dir))
```

## How it works

- **Getting into the app processes:** while `code` runs, covr is added to `R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES`, so every R process the tests start (shinytest2 uses callr, which passes it through) attaches covr. The new `.onAttach()` sets up the instrumentation when `COVR_SHINY_APP` is set and the process isn't the one that called `shiny_app_coverage()`.
- **Instrumenting the app's files:** Shiny's internal `sourceUTF8(file, envir)` is traced with `trace()`. When it returns, the functions it defined in the app's files (`app.R`, `ui.R`/`server.R`, `global.R`, `R/`) are instrumented in place. Shiny keeps srcrefs with the original line numbers (`#line` directives) even with `keep.source = FALSE`. This also happens in the calling process, so `testServer()` tests run by `test_app()` count too.
- **Inline server functions:** a server defined in `shinyApp(ui, function(...) ...)` or in `server.R` isn't bound to a name. Shiny passes it to `registerShinyDebugHook` (the hook RStudio uses for breakpoints), which covr defines in its package environment during `.onAttach()`, before that environment is locked. Shiny looks the hook up from its namespace, so it reaches the attached packages.
- **Saving:** an app process registers its trace (and pending marker) only once it instruments a function of the app, so other R processes don't leave empty traces. Traces are saved on exit and merged, and `covr_unsaved_trace` warns about app processes that were killed.
- Both hooks are Shiny internals. If `sourceUTF8()` no longer has `file` and `envir` arguments, covr warns rather than failing, and we can ask the Shiny team for exported hooks.

## Other changes

- The vignette's section on apps outside a package now uses `shiny_app_coverage()` instead of `file_coverage()`, and the README FAQ mentions it.
- `callr`, `shiny` and `shinytest2` added to Suggests.

## Verification

- `tests/testthat/test-shiny.R` (no browser needed) covers:
  - instrumentation in the calling process via `testServer()`, and that `sourceUTF8` is untraced afterwards;
  - a callr child that sources the app and calls the debug hook for an inline server, whose coverage is merged;
  - the warning for a killed app process.
- With shinytest2 0.5.1 and headless Chrome, `shiny_app_coverage()` on three apps gave the expected per-line counts, including uncovered functions:
  - an `app.R` app with an inline server and `R/` helpers;
  - a `ui.R`/`server.R`/`global.R`/`R/` app;
  - the vignette's example, combining an `AppDriver` test with a `testServer("../../")` test.
- Leaving out `app$stop()` produces the `covr_unsaved_trace` warning.
- Before #719 was merged: full `devtools::test()` passed (837), and R CMD check showed no new warnings or notes. On current `main`, the shiny tests pass and `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` is clean.

## Limitations

- As with `package_coverage()`, code outside functions (e.g. building the UI) isn't counted.
- Apps passed to `AppDriver$new()` as a function or app object aren't covered.

title: Drop DT and Bootstrap from the reports and add file_report_html()
description:
- **`file_report_html()`**: `file_report()` now wraps it in the standalone page, like `report()` wraps `report_html()`. Documented on the `file_report` page.
- **No Bootstrap**: the standalone page (`report_page()`) uses `page.css` for the centered column, fonts and heading sizes it got from Bootstrap 3. The vendored Bootstrap CSS and shims are removed, as are the Bootstrap authors in DESCRIPTION.
- **No DT**: the file list is a plain `<table>` built in R (`file_table()`), sorted by clicking a column header (`report.js`, with `aria-sort`), with the coverage bars as inline styles. DT is removed from Suggests, so `report()` only needs htmltools. The numeric columns are as narrow as their content and long paths wrap, so the table no longer spills out of the report.
- The initial order is the one `sort_file_stats()` computes (least covered first); DT re-sorted it by file name.
- The file links look up the file from the cell's `data-sort` value, as Quarto adds whitespace to the link text.

A report's dependencies are now only covr's report assets and highlight.js (40 KB in total, previously jQuery, DataTables, crosstalk, htmlwidgets and Bootstrap as well).

Fixes #709.

title: Add report_html() to include the coverage report in other documents
description:
`report_html()` returns the report shown by `report()` as an htmltools tag list, which can be printed in an R Markdown or Quarto chunk or saved with other content. `report()` now wraps it in the standalone page.

Making the report safe to embed required a few changes, found by rendering R Markdown (Bootstrap 3.3.5) and Quarto (Bootstrap 5) documents with two reports:

- **No Bootstrap in the report.** covr's Bootstrap 3.4.1 replaced the version of the document (including its bootswatch theme), and self-contained R Markdown documents failed to render because covr doesn't ship the glyphicon fonts. The tabs, file links and theme button now use covr's own classes, CSS and a small vanilla JS script (`report.js`). Only the standalone page loads Bootstrap's CSS; the unused `bootstrap.min.js` is removed.
- **Scoped styles.** All rules in `report.css` and the color CSS are under `.covr-report`, and the dark theme class is `covr-dark` instead of `dark`, so the report doesn't restyle the document. The page background for the standalone dark theme moved to `page.css`.
- **Assets as an html dependency.** `report.css`, `theme.js` and `report.js` (plus the color CSS in `head`) are a `covr-report` dependency, so they are included once and in the `<head>`; R Markdown drops `tags$head()` content and doesn't dedupe singletons across chunks.
- **highlight.js doesn't replace `hljs`.** covr's highlight.js 6.2 overwrote the document's `hljs`, breaking R Markdown's own highlighting (`hljs.configure is not a function`). It is now wrapped to set `covrHljs`, and its colors moved into `report.css` scoped to the report.
- **No repeated ids.** Files are found by `data-file` rather than `id`, tabs by `data-value` within their report, and the moon icon is a path instead of a masked circle.
- The DT table uses DT's `auto` height instead of a fixed 400-500px box.

The standalone `report()` and `file_report()` look the same as before (compared in a browser, light and dark).

Fixes #316.

title: Add a vignette on measuring the coverage of Shiny apps
description:
Fixes #277.

## What's already supported

Coverage of Shiny apps that are part of a package already works, including apps run by shinytest2. I checked this with a test package whose tests used `testServer()`, `AppDriver$new(<app object>)`, and `AppDriver$new(<app dir with app.R calling the package>)`. `package_coverage()` counted the code each of them exercised.

- An `AppDriver` app runs in a separate R process, which loads the instrumented package and saves its coverage when it exits.
- shinytest2's `AppDriver$stop()` already uses the workaround from this thread: it interrupts the app and waits 20 seconds under covr (`R_COVR`).
- Since #438, covr warns (`covr_unsaved_trace`) if an app is killed before it can save its coverage.

What users were missing was documentation, plus one gotcha: `AppDriver$new()` skips on CRAN, so shinytest2 tests are skipped under `package_coverage()` unless `NOT_CRAN=true`. GitHub Actions' `setup-r` sets it, but local runs don't.

## Changes

- New `vignette("shiny")`, covering apps in a package (`testServer()`, shinytest2, `app$stop()`, `NOT_CRAN`) and apps that aren't in a package (`file_coverage()` with `testServer()`).
- Links to the vignette from `?package_coverage` and a new README FAQ entry.
- NEWS bullet.

## Verification

- I extracted the vignette's code into a package and ran `package_coverage()` with headless Chrome and shinytest2 0.5.1. Coverage was 100%, including `app_ui()`, which only the shinytest2 tests call.
- The standalone `file_coverage()` example also gave 100%.
- The vignette renders, and `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` passes.

title: Measure the coverage of test files with `include_tests = TRUE`
description:
With `package_coverage(include_tests = TRUE)`, the coverage also includes the R files in `tests/`, whatever framework runs them. You can use it to:

- find test helpers that are never used,
- see tests that don't run, for example because they are skipped,
- give `tests/` its own Codecov components or flags, since test files are named by path like package files (`tests/testthat/test-foo.R`).

The default is `FALSE`, so existing coverage results don't change.

## How it works

Test code isn't in the package namespace, so covr can't instrument it when the package loads. Instead:

1. **Choosing files:** every `.R` file under `tests/` (recursively) is included, except the ones listed in `.covrignore`. That's where users list files the tests read as data, such as fixtures.
2. **Instrumenting:** the main process instruments each file with `trace_calls()` in a test-file mode. That mode:
   - keys traces by the path relative to the package,
   - keeps srcrefs, so `covr.record_tests` still identifies tests,
   - doesn't instrument the arguments of `quote()`, `bquote()`, `expression()`, `alist()`, `substitute()` and `expect_snapshot()`. Instrumenting `expect_snapshot()` code would change what the snapshot records, so those tests would fail.
3. **Running:** the instrumented code is saved in the install directory. Each installed file is replaced by a one-line stub, `covr:::run_traced_file()`. The stub runs the code where the file would have run, prints top-level values for scripts directly in `tests/` as `R CMD BATCH` does, and saves its counts when the process exits.
4. **Merging:** zero-count traces from the main process are merged with the saved counts, so files and lines that never run show as uncovered.

Apart from the `expect_snapshot()` entry in that list, nothing depends on a particular test framework.

## Limitations (documented)

- R files the tests read as data, rather than run, must be listed in `.covrignore`. This includes snapshots saved by `expect_snapshot_file()`.
- Test frameworks may report failures in test files at line 1, because the file they open is the stub.
- Code inside other functions that capture their arguments shows the extra counting calls when deparsed.

## Tests

- New fixture `tests/testthat/TestTestFiles` and `tests/testthat/test-test_files.R`. They check:
  - test files are left out by default,
  - line values for used and unused helpers, skipped tests and plain scripts,
  - code inside `expect_snapshot()` and `quote()` isn't instrumented,
  - a file listed in `.covrignore` is left alone.
- I checked that the tests fail if `expect_snapshot` is removed from the list, or if the `.covrignore` file isn't used.
- Full suite after rebasing onto `main`: `[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 826 ]`.

Fixes #541.

title: Add `to_badge()` to make coverage badges locally
description:
Several people have built their own way to get a coverage badge without Codecov or Coveralls (shields.io URLs built from `percent_coverage()`, workflows that edit an SVG, covr2gh). This adds it to covr.

`to_badge(cov, filename = "coverage.svg", label = "coverage")` writes a flat SVG badge with the percent coverage, made locally with no network calls.

- The percentage is that of `percent_coverage()`, rounded down so only fully covered code shows 100%.
- Colors: green at 90% or more, yellow at 75% or more, red below. These are the thresholds `report()` uses. Coverage with no lines of code shows `unknown` on a gray badge.
- Text widths come from Verdana's 11px glyph advance widths, read from the font's `hmtx` table. The `<text>` elements set `textLength`, so the text still fits when the badge is drawn in DejaVu Sans or another fallback font.
- The label is XML-escaped and sets the width of the left side of the badge.

The README gains a "Coverage badge without a coverage service" section. It has a GitHub Actions example that force-pushes the badge to a single-commit `badges` branch, and a raw URL to use in the README.

Fixes #634.

title: Measure coverage of installed packages
description:
`package_coverage()` now accepts the path to an installed package, so the package source isn't needed (#638):

```r
remotes::install_github(
  "user/pkg",
  INSTALL_opts = c("--install-tests", "--with-keep.source")
)
covr::package_coverage(system.file(package = "pkg"))
```

Previously this silently returned no coverage. `R CMD INSTALL` copies an installed package, and its srcrefs (when it was installed with `--with-keep.source`) point to the source it was installed from, so `filter_non_package_files()` dropped every file.

For an installed package (one with `Meta/package.rds`), `package_coverage()` now:

- uses the source directory recorded in the srcrefs as the package path, for filtering and for relative file names (`R/foo.R`). The source doesn't have to exist anymore; reports use the source lines in the srcrefs.
- skips `clean_objects()`, `clean_gcov()`, gcov and `.covrignore`, so it doesn't touch the installed or source directory. Compiled code isn't covered.
- errors if the package was installed without tests (when running tests) or without srcrefs, which would otherwise give no or empty coverage.

Fixes #638.

title: Let objects used in tests be garbage collected, and record tests without srcrefs once, with `covr.record_tests`
description:
Both problems in #627 only happen with `options(covr.record_tests = TRUE)`. Without that option, websocket's tests pass and bitops' coverage takes a few seconds, with covr 3.6.5 and with main. The `-O0 --coverage` flags explain the different `.so` sizes the issue mentions, since gcov needs them, but they don't cause either failure.

| | covr 3.6.5 | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| websocket tests, `record_tests` | 3 failures (`test-client.R:209`, `:225`, `:443`) | 1 failure (`:209`) | pass |
| bitops `consistency.R`, `record_tests` | doesn't finish (> 5 min) | doesn't finish (> 5 min) | ~30 s |

## websocket: objects used in tests were never garbage collected

`update_current_test()` held onto the environment that the last test call ran in (`.current_test$src_env`). For websocket that's the `local()` environment holding the `WebSocket`, so the object's finalizer never ran. covr now references that environment only through a weak reference, created in C with `R_MakeWeakRef()`.

The last test call (`.current_test$src_call`) also held onto the environments of functions inside it, e.g. an R6 active binding called from the test. It's now the call from the recorded trace, whose functions already have their environments removed (#692), and it is compared with `identical(ignore.environment = TRUE)`.

## bitops: tests without srcrefs were recorded once per run

When tests have no srcrefs, e.g. scripts in `tests/` run with `R CMD BATCH`, `current_test_index()` finds a test by comparing call stacks with `identical(t[], .current_test$trace)`. The `t[]` was meant to drop the `call_count` attribute (#528), but `t[]` keeps attributes. So no test ever matched, every run was recorded as a new test, and each lookup scanned all earlier ones. bitops' `consistency.R` calls the package about 125,000 times in a loop, which made the time quadratic. The attribute is now removed before comparing.

`strip_function_envs()` (#692, not released yet) runs on every frame of each test and walked every call in R. It now only walks calls that contain a function, which C checks. That brings bitops from ~140 s with just the matching fix down to ~30 s.

## Tests

- Tests without srcrefs: `for (i in 1:3) { a(); b() }` run through `package_coverage(type = "none")` records 2 tests with call counts 1, 2, 3. Before the fix it recorded 6 tests, each with call count 1.
- Garbage collection: R6 objects used through a method and through an active binding inside `local()` are each finalized by the `gc()` right after. Before the fix neither was.

Both tests fail on main and pass here. The full suite passes (821). I also checked against the CRAN websocket 1.4.4 and bitops 1.1-0 sources using `package_coverage(type = "tests")` with `record_tests`.

## Not changed

Environments placed directly in a call, e.g. `do.call(f, list(r6_object))`, or a list built in C such as websocket's event, are still kept in the recorded traces, like before. websocket's traces contain none, so its tests aren't affected.

Fixes #627.

title: Only list a method's own lines in `to_cobertura()`
description:
`to_cobertura()` picked the lines of each `<method>` by function name across **all** files (`which(df$functions == fun_name)`), and computed the method's `line-rate` across all files too. R6 methods are named by the method name alone, so classes in different files that share a method name (`initialize`, `set_data`, `run_search`, ...) listed each other's lines under every class. Codecov merges method lines into the file's lines, which explains what #629 reports:

- line numbers past the end of the file (577 in a 494-line file)
- roxygen and comment lines flagged as uncovered (lines from other files land on them)
- a different percentage than `print(cov)` (62.39% on Codecov vs 100% from covr)

#691 had already fixed the file and overall totals, but not the per-method lines. Methods are now built from the rows of their own file only.

### Repro (before this PR)

Two R6 classes, `A` in `R/a.R` (6 lines) and `B` in `R/b.R` (`initialize` at line 43), with tests that only call `A$new()`. `print(cov)` gave `R/a.R: 100.00%`, but the cobertura `initialize` method under `R/a.R` listed line 43 with `hits="0"` and `line-rate="0.5"`. With this PR it lists only line 3 with `line-rate="1"`.

Includes a regression test that fails before the change and passes after.

Fixes #629.

title: Fall back to gcov's text output if its JSON output can't be used
description:
Follow-up to #712 (#609). The JSON format is chosen once from `gcov --help`; if a gcov version we haven't tested advertises `--json-format` but writes its output under a different name or in a structure we can't parse, that file's compiled coverage was lost (or covr errored).

Now, per source file, if gcov wrote no `.gcov.json.gz` or parsing it fails, gcov is run again with `-a` text output and the existing text parser. Errors from gcov itself (#690) still error; only missing or unparseable JSON triggers the fallback.

Tests (TestCompiled, real gcov 13): the compiled coverage is identical to the text path when `parse_gcov_json()` errors and when gcov writes no JSON. The test fails without the fallback; the full suite passes with the branch installed.

title: Use gcov's JSON output for compiled code coverage
description:
`run_gcov()` now runs `gcov --json-format` when gcov supports it, and reads the structured `.gcov.json.gz` output with jsonlite in the new `parse_gcov_json()`. Before, it always parsed gcov's text output with regular expressions.

## Details

- **Detection:** covr runs `gcov --help` (with `covr.gcov_args`) and checks whether it lists `--json-format`. gcc >= 9 does. llvm-cov (the gcov on macOS) and gcc < 9 don't, so they still go through the existing text parser with `gcov -a`.
- **Grouped functions:** gcc's text output prints the combined lines of grouped functions (e.g. a template instantiated twice in one object), then repeats each function's lines between `------------------` separators. JSON mode only has the per-function lines (checked with gcc 13), so `parse_gcov_json()` adds up the counts per line.
- **Bug fix in the text parser:** `parse_gcov()` matched the repeated per-function lines as well as the combined ones, and `merge_values()` sums duplicates, so these lines were counted twice. The per-function entries could also undo `covr.gcov_partial = "uncovered"`. Every gcc >= 8 user of the released covr is affected. The text parser now skips those sections. On CRAN's RcppRoll (with its examples run) the two parsers previously gave 1041 vs 6017 entries; they now give identical coverage data frames.
- **Partial lines:** these come from gcov's `unexecuted_block` field, and still respect `options(covr.gcov_partial)` (#604, #610).
- **Source paths:** relative source paths are resolved against the `current_working_directory` that gcov records.
- **Behavior change:** lines only reached by C++ exceptions (`=====` in the text output, e.g. a `catch` block that never ran) are reported in the JSON output with a count of 0, so they now count as not covered. Before, they were dropped. The text parser now does the same, so you get the same results whichever gcov you use.

## Tests

- `parse_gcov_json()` unit test: sums grouped function lines, applies `covr.gcov_partial`, resolves relative paths and leaves out files outside the package.
- `parse_gcov()` unit test: per-function sections of grouped functions are skipped, including with `covr.gcov_partial = "uncovered"`.
- `gcov_json_supported()` unit test, with gcc help output, help output without JSON, and a gcov that errors.
- New integration test: `TestCompiled` gives identical `as.data.frame()` coverage with the JSON and text parsers. (It has no template instantiated twice in one object, so the grouped-function case is covered by the unit tests and the RcppRoll comparison above.)
- The empty-gcov-output warning test used `covr.gcov_args = "-n"`, but gcc 13 writes the JSON file even with `-n`, so the test now mocks `gcov_run()` instead.

Full suite passes locally with gcc 13.3 (`[ FAIL 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 795 ]`).

Fixes #609.

title: Name S4 methods after their generic and signature
description:
S4 methods were named by their keys in the methods table, e.g. `numeric#character`, which don't include the generic, so `print(x, group = "functions")` and `tally_coverage(by = "function")` couldn't show which generic a method belongs to, and a method for `show()` was named just like its class.

Methods are now named like their Rd aliases (as roxygen2 generates them from `@generic` and `@defined`), e.g. `show,TestS4-method` and `print2,TestS4,character-method`.

Fixes #417.

title: Add missing blank lines between NEWS bullets
description: Three bullets in the development section lost the blank line before them in merges. Only the development section is touched, so it doesn't conflict with the open PRs that add bullets at the top.

title: Shorten error and warning messages following the tidyverse style guide
description:
Rewrites covr's errors and warnings to start with a short problem statement followed by `✖`/`ℹ` bullets, following https://style.tidyverse.org/errors.html. In particular the warning about processes that didn't save their coverage is now three short lines.

- Adds internal `covr_abort()` and `covr_warn()` helpers that format messages with `cli::format_error()` / `cli::format_warning()` (no rlang needed) while keeping custom condition classes.
- Updates messages for package lookup, trace files, installation, `type`, gcov, icc, `# nocov` ranges, `line_exclusions`, Coveralls uploads, `report()` dependencies, report colors and system commands.

title: Don't save lazy-load promises of srcfiles in traces (#602)
description:
Fixes #602.

## Cause

`gdb` on the reprex from the issue ([dgkf/reprex-covr-segfault](https://github.com/dgkf/reprex-covr-segfault)) shows the crash happens inside arrow's ALTREP `Serialized_state()`. It is reached from `saveRDS(.counters)` in covr's exit finalizer:

```
#0  arrow::r::altrep::...AltrepVectorBase<...>::Length (alt=...) at altrep.cpp:114
#1  arrow::r::altrep::...AltrepVectorPrimitive<14>::Materialize at altrep.cpp:191
#2  arrow::r::altrep::...::Serialized_state at altrep.cpp:158
#3  WriteItem (...) at serialize.c:1053
...
#30 R_Serialize
...
#40 R_RunWeakRefFinalizer
#42 R_RunExitFinalizers
```

The counters reach the arrow data through the srcrefs:

1. The srcfiles of an installed package are restored from its lazy-load database. Their `lines` and `parseData` are promises (`makeLazy()` in `lazyLoadDBexec()`).
2. Those promises are evaluated in the `lazyLoadDBexec()` frame, whose `envenv` holds every environment restored from the database. That includes `runtime` and the closure environment of `buildtime_fastmap` from the reprex.
3. `parseData` is usually never forced, so serializing a counter's srcref also serializes the contents of all of those environments.
4. On exit, arrow's finalizers run before covr's (R runs newer weak refs first). Serializing the ALTREP columns then dereferences arrays that have already been freed.

This explains the patterns in the reprex. A fastmap in the global environment is serialized as a reference, so it was fine. An `if` in `.onLoad` used to make older covr call `getParseData()`, which forced the promise; R drops a promise's environment once it is forced. With `covr.record_tests = TRUE` the srcrefs in the recorded calls hit the same problem.

## Fix

`save_trace()` now saves `portable_srcfiles(.counters)`:

- It serializes the counters with a `refhook` that replaces each srcfile environment with an id.
- It then unserializes them with a `refhook` that returns a copy of the srcfile. The copy holds the values of its bindings, so `lines` is loaded, but not `parseData`.
- The copies are memoized by address, so all the `srcfilealias`es of a package share one copy of the srcfile with the package's lines.

Because the `refhook` finds srcfiles anywhere in the object, this also covers the calls recorded with `covr.record_tests`. The trace files also get smaller: in the reprex with `mtcars` stored in the fastmap, a trace file went from 22.5 kB to 2.2 kB.

`parseData` is only used when tracing (`impute_srcref()`), not when merging traces or reporting.

## Verification

- With the arrow reprex, `package_coverage()` succeeds for every scenario that crashed before (parquet × runtime/buildtime/lazy-fastmap, with and without `if (TRUE) {}` in `.onLoad`) and with `covr.record_tests = TRUE`. HEAD still segfaults in these scenarios.
- `tally_coverage()` for the parquet/global scenario, which didn't crash before, is the same as HEAD's.
- The new test in `test-covr.R` fails on HEAD (the package environment gets serialized) and passes with the fix.
- `devtools::test()` passes with this covr installed: 781 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped.

title: Register the trace in an onLoad hook (fixes test-coverage slowdown)
description:
The test-coverage job's coverage step went from ~80 s to ~600 s, starting at #668.

**Cause:** #668 replaced the load script's `reg.finalizer(...)` line with `covr:::register_trace(ns, ...)`, which runs while the package is still being lazy-loaded and so loads covr then, instead of in the onLoad hook as before. When covr measures its own coverage, that covr is the instrumented copy, and in each subprocess that loads a fixture package `getParseData()` during tracing went from 0.06 s to 3.3 s (Rprof of the TestSummary fixture's test process). Normal use isn't affected: instrumenting withr takes 1.3 s before and after #668.

**Fix:** call `register_trace()` from an onLoad hook, like `trace_environment()`.

**Verification (local, R 4.6.2):**
- `test-cobertura.R` under covr-on-covr: 19.0 s → 5.1 s.
- Full shimmed covr-on-covr `package_coverage()` with `CI=true`: 96 s (was ~470–550 s locally, ~600 s on CI), coverage unchanged at 76.5%.
- Full suite with the branch installed: 789 pass, 0 fail (including #668's tests for unsaved traces and forked workers).

title: Fix syntax highlighting in file_report()
description:
`file_report()` loaded Bootstrap's JavaScript and ran its highlighting with `$()`, but doesn't include jQuery, so both failed (`Bootstrap's JavaScript requires jQuery`, `$ is not defined`) and the source wasn't highlighted.

- The highlighting script uses `document.querySelectorAll()` instead, so it doesn't need jQuery. `report()` uses the same script.
- `file_report()` leaves out Bootstrap's JavaScript (`fluid_page(js = FALSE)`), which is only used for the tabs in `report()`. The CSS and the old-IE shims stay.
- Long titles, like the file paths in `file_report()`, now wrap instead of pushing the dark mode button out of the column.

Checked in headless Chromium: `file_report()` highlights its source with no page errors, and `report()`'s tabs and highlighting still work.

title: Document using file_coverage() on files from a package
description: Fixes #600. Adds a short section to `?file_coverage`: load the package and pass `parent_env = asNamespace("pkg")` so the package's other functions are found; calls from other package files aren't counted; `devtools::test_coverage_active_file()` covers one package file without that limitation. Checked on a small package: without `parent_env` the test fails with `could not find function`; with it, 100% coverage of the file.
